title: The alternate life you regret was never guaranteed
headline: The alternate life you regret was never guaranteed
caption: If only I had told her. But was the imagined outcome ever guaranteed? JT questions the certainty we give to a relationship that never happened.
why: A missed-romance example challenges a familiar kind of regret and lands on the uncertainty hidden in the story we tell ourselves.
hook: You can't say, if I had to, you know, you say, well,
ends: What is, is. Okay? And that's just the way that it is.
transcript: You can't say, if I had to, you know, you say, well, I was in love with a girl, and I was afraid to tell her. And it turned out she was in love with me, and she was waiting for me to tell her. So if I had told her that I loved her, then we would have been together. False. False. You might believe that today, and she might believe that today. You might sit at a table with a cup of coffee looking into her eyes, and both of you fully believe that if you would only have the balls to speak up, you would have been together. And that is an absolutely false idea. There are so many possibilities of how that could have played out. But in reality, what happened, happened. What is, is. Okay? And that's just the way that it is.

title: Why did everyone arrive at the gas station together
headline: Why did everyone arrive at the gas station together?
caption: Before smartphones, JT worked overnight at a gas station. He remembers three rushes a night, at changing times, with everyone seeming to arrive together. Even the staff joked about it.
why: An ordinary overnight job becomes a small mystery: customers arrive in bursts even though the bursts shift from night to night.
hook: My first job, I was an overnight gas station attendant. And we
ends: on the phone. It was a joke. We weren't serious about it.
transcript: My first job, I was an overnight gas station attendant. And we would get three rushes a night. But the funny thing is, it wasn't at the same time. We would just get three rushes. So one night, it might be 12 o'clock. The next night, it might be 1230. One o'clock, 110, 145, okay, for the first rush. And everyone would show up. This was before people had cell phones in their pockets. This was back when there were pay phones, right? This was back when very few people had personal computers even. So there was no GPS guiding people except the GPS in their mind. And it was overnight. So sometimes people would just wake up, right? And 10 people would wake up or roll out of the bar and go to the gas station at the same time. And then the next rush would be like 13 people. Then it'd be like seven or eight people, right? But it was always at the same time, even though the time was different. The third rush could be 545. It could be 6 o'clock. It could be 630. Everyone would show up at the same fucking time. Every single night. And everyone would joke about it who had that job. They would joke about it that, like, someone was sending out a radar signal or something, you know, or calling people on the phone. It was a joke. We weren't serious about it.

title: What secret societies are really filtering for
headline: What secret societies are really filtering for
episode_title: Defining Remote Viewing:  June, and the video
caption: Blue is the best color. Next level, red. Then yellow. JT on why some secret societies make members contradict themselves at every level, and who that filters for.
why: Re-cut (Matt, 2026-11-16): the first cut started mid-thought. It now opens on the secret-society setup and ends on the filter payoff, so the blue-red-yellow lesson makes sense on its own.
hook: But the real secret of secret societies is the real reason that someone goes to
ends: It's, it's filtering for people with those traits, persistent predatory personality traits.
transcript: But the real secret of secret societies is the real reason that someone goes to, and I'm not talking about every secret society, but one of the things you learn if you ever study that subject is that there'll be this gradient of levels. And at each level, they'll contradict themselves. So at one level, they'll, you know, I don't have to confabulate something here, but like at one level, they'll teach you like blue is the best color. Then the next level, they're like, no, no, blue is a sucky color. Red is the best color. Don't you agree? And if you agree, they're like, okay, well, we'll do the next level. And then like yellow is the best color. You were just lying, right? And you're like, oh yeah, okay, I agree. Yellow is the best color. So what they're looking for there is someone who is willing and capable of contradicting themselves for personal gain. Someone who has no moral center, no consistent moral center. And the ultimate, if you look at a secret society, like, you know, you're not going to say 100% of people at the top are psychopaths. But a much higher degree of people who are psychopaths at the top, because it's a, it's a filter mechanism, right? It's, it's filtering for people with those traits, persistent predatory personality traits.

headline: Three different dinner predictions, one advertised success
episode_title: Comet 3i Atlas, test for mankind or the Remote Viewing Community?

hook: If we were viewing a dinner, right, and one viewer said spaghetti,

title: Weeks of work on a sand mandala, then a broom
headline: Weeks of work on a sand mandala, then a broom
episode_title: The Kalachakra Tantric Sand Mandala... a metaphor for life

why: Re-cut (Matt, 2026-11-16): the first cut never said what was being made. It now opens by naming the Tibetan sand mandala, then the weeks of work and the broom.
hook: A Tibetan sand mandala. If you are all familiar, they draw out a very elaborate image
ends: painstaking work to make. They'll just sweep it up in a pile.
transcript: A Tibetan sand mandala. If you are all familiar, they draw out a very elaborate image, a mandala, which has psychological properties. Mandalas all have psychological properties. And then they painstakingly, by hand, trace the image with colored sand. And they create these beautiful, vivid mandalas, which symbolize the world or healing. They have like a ritual component to them. But they also all generally symbolize the world. And they'll sometimes have a goddess in the middle who could be Tara or it could be Kuan Yin, the goddess of mercy. And then at the end of this process, which usually takes about three weeks or a month, they have a viewing. And then for a few days. And then on like the third day, they'll have everyone come in and they will take just take brooms and just sweep that unbelievable piece of art that took hundreds of hours of painstaking work to make. They'll just sweep it up in a pile.

title: Why Neanderthal skeletons look like rodeo clowns
headline: Why Neanderthal skeletons look like rodeo clowns
caption: Humans hunted by chasing animals until they tired. Neanderthals, JT says, hid among the herd and jumped them, and their skeletons show the same damage as a career rodeo clown.
why: Replaces the dropped MacBook story (Matt, 2026-11-16). A surprising, self-contained idea: it opens by naming Neanderthals, contrasts endurance hunting with ambush hunting, and lands on the rodeo-clown image. Space not otherwise used in week 4. Trimmed (Matt, 2026-11-16): now ends before JT's next sentence starts ("However, we do know they experienced empathy..."). A longer version that finishes that thought (89.7 s) is in /Users/mtmccarthy/peak-mind-shorts/week-04-dropped/.
hook: I know with Neanderthals particularly, right, when they find their skeletons,
ends: And so they didn't live, they didn't live very long for that reason.
transcript: I know with Neanderthals particularly, right, when they find their skeletons, I think that they tend to live, if they can, about the same length as a human being, or at least 50 years. However, most of them didn't. And the reason that is often given is that they had a strange hunting style, which was more of an ambush hunting style. The human beings get together and chase the animals down, which is our advantage. And then when the animals are tired, you know, we're not tired because we're endurance runners. And then we are able to kill the animals. What the Neanderthals did was kind of blend in with groups of animals and then, on a predetermined time, jump on them and stab them to death. That's what's believed. And there's a tremendous amount of evidence because the average Neanderthal skeleton shows the same type and extent of damage as a rodeo clown. Like, very, very similar damage that that is sustained by a rodeo clown during his career. And... Pretty beaten, huh? Yeah. From getting thrown around by the animals, kicked and thrown and stomped on. And so they didn't live, they didn't live very long for that reason.

title: The character changes, but the book was already whole
headline: The character changes, but the book was already whole
caption: JT's take on Jung's Unus Mundi: a deeper part of your mind may see your life the way you see a finished book. The character grows as you read, but every page was already there.
why: Expanded (Matt, 2026-11-16): now opens with why JT reaches for the book (our deeper mind sees our life like one). Ends on "as solid as that book" at Matt's pick. Captions now read "Unus Mundi" instead of whisper's "doing this Monday".
hook: I think that our unconscious mind is a term that we use to describe our mind on that level in the Unus Mundi
ends: the experience we're having here right now, this dream, right, is as solid as that book.
transcript: I think that our unconscious mind is a term that we use to describe our mind on that level in the Unus Mundi. And I think that our mind on that level in the Unus Mundi is conscious a little bit, even in its unconscious state, and is aware of our lives like a book. So we read a book and we say, well, this character has experienced a lot of growth. But of course, the character didn't experience any growth. That's an illusion that the book conjures in our minds, right? Because the book is 300 pages with a cover on the top and a cover on the bottom. You slam on the desk and everything that was in that book was there the day you bought it, the day you opened it. And it's only a perception that causes us to think there was any change involved. It's one solid thing, including the words in the story. On that level, the level of Unus Mundi, the experience we're having here right now, this dream, right, is as solid as that book.

title: What surprised him about using a wheelchair
headline: What surprised him about using a wheelchair
caption: JT spent years using a wheelchair. What stayed with him was how often strangers responded with hostility. This is his account of an experience he had not expected.
why: Re-cut (Matt, 2026-11-16): the first cut opened on "that's not what happens" without saying what. It now starts on the hope that people feel compassion for the sick, then the wheelchair years that showed otherwise.
hook: A lot of us would like people to feel compassion and love and sympathy for the sick.
ends: me. Just in my presence, if not more than 10 to 1.
transcript: A lot of us would like people to feel compassion and love and sympathy for the sick. But if you've ever been visibly sick or disabled, you will know that that's not what happens at all. I mean, if you're in that position, you're not necessarily looking for people to be super sympathetic. But what will surprise you is that you will experience far more hostility than compassion. And it's something you may not have considered prior to that event happening. But, you know, I was in a wheelchair for a few years. And I would either have people angrily, sort of angrily ignore me or, like, ignore me with, like, with intent. Or I would have people react in a hostile way to me. But when I was in public in the wheelchair, for every one person who was kind and compassionate, and I'm not saying people are required to. I'm just saying this is what happened. For every one person that would demonstrate kindness or compassion to me, at least 10 people would be visibly hostile to me. Just in my presence, if not more than 10 to 1.

title: The spiritual benefit of a spare light bulb
headline: The spiritual benefit of a spare light bulb
episode_title: The Kalachakra Tantric Sand Mandala... a metaphor for life
caption: The root of clutter is attachment, but letting go does not mean throwing out useful things. JT's example: the spiritual benefit of a spare light bulb is using it when you need one.
why: Re-cut (Matt, 2026-11-16): the first cut opened on "people are pretty good with that" with no subject. It now opens on clutter and attachment, then the light bulb line and the mission.
hook: A lot of us clutter. I'm sure that no one else here has this problem, but I do.
ends: to sweep it up and to send it out into the ocean.
transcript: A lot of us clutter. I'm sure that no one else here has this problem, but I do. And the root of clutter is attachment. Whereas, you know, other people are pretty good with that, right? They're pretty good with cleaning out the clutter and letting it go. That Marie Kondo. I'm not telling people that there's a spiritual benefit to getting rid of unused light bulbs. There isn't. The spiritual benefit of unused light bulbs is using them when you need a light bulb. It definitely shouldn't be purging your life of things that can be useful. But the things that no longer have a use to you are a way of sending that energy out into the world, are a way of releasing attachment and getting back to the point where you're focused on that mission, right? You built a life around that mission and you acquired goods and you acquired friends and you acquired a family and you acquire a lot of things along the way, but that mission is what's important. And when it comes time to pursue that mission elsewhere, then it's time to sweep it up and to send it out into the ocean.
edit: Two pieces of the source: 2372.25 to 2380.2 ("A lot of us clutter ... the root of clutter is attachment") joined to 2435.95 to 2499.53, which drops an aside on hoarding and keepsakes.

title: Dolphins at the United Nations

transcript: What happened was, Lilly started to experience extraterrestrial communications, according to himself. He experienced three disembodied non-human intelligence that referred to themselves as the Earth, or he referred to them at least as, the Earth Coincidence Control Office. And those disembodied non-human intelligence told him he had to quit his job, he had to divorce his wife, he had to move to St. Thomas in the Virgin Islands, and he had to figure out how to speak to dolphins. And that because of his work, dolphins would one day be admitted into the United Nations, and then you'll learn how to communicate with dolphins, and then you can speak to the aliens. The reason you need to learn how to do this is because the universe is filled with intelligence, and that intelligence is often not friendly to human beings.

title: Why assume an alien civilization has billions of people
headline: Why assume an alien civilization has billions of people?
caption: Does older automatically mean more populous? JT asks why hypothetical alien civilizations are so often imagined as endless billions.
why: Re-cut (Matt, 2026-11-16): the first cut opened on "That assumption" without saying which. It now starts on the assumption itself, exponential population growth, then the right-whale comparison.
hook: Here's another assumption. Exponential growth. Not just exponential growth in technology,
ends: a time where there are a billion right whales in the ocean.
transcript: Here's another assumption. Exponential growth. Not just exponential growth in technology, but exponential growth in population. Because that's what's happened on Earth. That's what's happened to us, right? Where in a very short time, we've surged to six to eight billion people. I happen to believe it's less than eight billion. That's why I say six to eight billion. But you can say eight billion, right? So in a very short time, a couple hundred years, we've grown exponentially. So when people look into space, when they look for the evidence of this civilization, they're looking for the evidence of billions of lives. Hundreds of billions, trillions of lives. Xenu, right? Up there in the center of the galaxy with planets everywhere filled with billions and billions of people. That assumption is another one that's not substantiated. There is absolutely no reason to believe that alien civilizations would experience exponential, continuous exponential population growth. Or that other species, right, would have as many people, would have the same population numbers, right? Like that they would have billions and billions of people. Like there are species on this planet, you know, like whales, right? I mean, like right whales, like there's not, there's never been a time where there are a billion right whales in the ocean.

title: Finding what you want to hear is not research
headline: Finding what you want to hear is not research
caption: Start with the primary source. JT explains why searching until a website agrees with you is not the same as researching a question.
why: Opens with a practical research step and contrasts finding a source with collecting agreeable websites.
hook: When you have a question, you identify what the primary source is,
ends: to find that person, those people, and listen to what they say.
transcript: When you have a question, you identify what the primary source is, and you look for the answer there. And at some point, people stop doing that. And we can blame millennials all we want, but I think this Brett Freeman is a Gen X. So obviously, it didn't just start with millennials. Obviously, there were people in my generation who abandoned basic research. People say they're researching, but they're actually engaging in confirmation bias, right? Because they're looking for websites that tell them what they're interested in, right? And tell them what they want to know. That's not research. That's just confirmation bias. Because they can't identify what the primary source is, okay? So you have to start with the primary source. You have to know who knows. And you've got to find that person, those people, and listen to what they say.

title: Not every coincidence is a message to you
headline: Not every coincidence is a message to you
caption: Finding patterns is one thing. Believing every event is about you is another. JT cautions against losing that distinction when exploring synchronicity.
why: Puts an essential limit on the show's synchronicity theme, with a concrete birthday-versus-revolution example a stranger can follow.
hook: The danger in this thinking, no one should really go down this
ends: if they're just not the right type of person to do it.
transcript: The danger in this thinking, no one should really go down this path if they have a predisposition to certain types of delusions, because in certain cases with mental illness, people develop delusions of personal reference. And in that case, they have a predisposition to seeing events outside themselves as being related to themselves. So there's ideas of personal reference, which is like, gee, isn't it weird that on my birthday, in history, there have been three revolutions. Now, I'm not saying it's my birthday. I'm saying I'm going to just pick that randomly, right? That's an idea of personal representation. But if someone says, or if someone believes, like, every time they have a birthday, they're causing a revolution, that's a delusion of personal representation. And that's something that can happen to people if they pursue looking into synchronicities and the unconscious before they're ready, or if they're just not the right type of person to do it.
